idiom_name: context.Context request-scoped value with an unexported key type, read through a typed accessor
implementation_notes: Go has no ambient storage, so the idiomatic carrier is context.Context, passed as the first argument of every request-scoped function: the boundary middleware derives a child with context.WithValue(ctx, key, principal), where key is an unexported struct type so no other package can collide with it - the convention the standard library's userip example documents and the 2014 Go blog describes for exactly this case (request-scoped values such as the identity of the end user and authorization tokens). Guards read it through a small typed accessor that returns (principal, ok) and fail closed when ok is false, so the classic container plus holder is replaced by this convention; the 2021 follow-up article fixes the discipline (pass the context as an argument rather than storing it in structs). A single immutable *SecurityContext under one key is still the right move when several attributes (tenant, scopes, authentication method) travel together, because many keys make the context unreadable.
pitfalls: context.WithValue returns a child context: a handler that keeps using the parent variable silently drops the principal for everything downstream.
The key must be an unexported type (an empty struct is typical) and the value safe for concurrent use; exported or string keys collide across packages.
The context is for request-scoped data only - not for optional parameters or mutable state - and a guard must still verify what it reads rather than trusting a value another package could have set.
